issues.detail: The two examples are prose descriptions that reference earlier manifests rather than showing full runnable commands and outputs end to end.

scenarios.name: canary-release-with-qa-header
scenarios.rationale: Both supply networking.istio.io/v1 manifests with the header match first, a 90/10 split, 5xx retries and istioctl analyze; B names the subsets stable/canary as the rubric asks and also uses istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/web-app -n shop, while A names the subsets v1/v2 and uses a placeholder deploy name in its proxy-config command.

scenarios.name: safe-strict-mtls-rollout
scenarios.rationale: B follows the rubric closely: PERMISSIVE first, confirm callers are in the mesh, STRICT in istio-system, and an ALLOW policy with principal cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/frontend, GET/POST, /api/* and app: api-service, plus warnings about non-mesh pods and deny-all. A is thorough but flips STRICT namespace by namespace instead of mesh-wide in istio-system, and it uses a placeholder namespace in the principal instead of shop. Its dry-run and gotchas are useful extras but depart from the rubric.

scenarios.name: gateway-api-ingress-and-tracing
scenarios.rationale: Response A matches the rubric: it installs the Gateway API CRDs, creates a Gateway with gatewayClassName istio and an HTTPS listener that terminates TLS with a certificateRef, adds an HTTPRoute with a PathPrefix /api rule and a default frontend backend, and enables tracing through a Telemetry resource at 1% with a zipkin extensionProvider. Response B uses the classic Istio Gateway and VirtualService instead, with no Gateway API CRDs, no gatewayClassName and no HTTPRoute, so it only meets the tracing part of the rubric.
